Language Change. The process by which languages evolve over time, altering their sounds, grammar, and vocabulary. Studied through diachronic linguistics, language change operates through mechanisms like sound shifts, analogy, and social factors. William Labov pioneered the modern understanding of how language changes, demonstrating that variation and change happen in real time through social forces, not in sudden leaps.

Languages are always changing. No language is static. This is a universal feature of human communication. Sound change occurs regularly. English lost its final "e" in many words, and vowel shifts like the Great Vowel Shift in Middle English transformed pronunciation. Grammatical change involves shifts in morphology and syntax. English lost its inflectional case endings, and changes in word order patterns followed. Lexical change brings new words through borrowing and neologism while removing old ones through obsolescence. Rates vary by social prestige.

Variation precedes change. Labov showed that linguistic change happens incrementally, visible in apparent-time studies of living speakers. Social factors drive change. Younger speakers, women, and lower-status groups often lead in adopting innovations. Sound changes spread gradually through a language area, not uniformly. Geography and social networks matter. Regularity characterizes language change. Systematic sound changes typically apply consistently across a class of words, following the Neogrammarian principle. Internal motivations for change include analogical reanalysis, where "pea" emerged as a singular from "pease" as a collective, and phonetic simplification. Frequency effects shape change patterns. Irregular verbs often resist change, so "go," "went," and "gone" remain irregular. High-frequency words stabilize while rare words shift faster. Functional pressure can drive grammar changes. The loss of case endings increases reliance on word order, triggering syntactic reorganization. Sociolinguistics is the field that studies language change in social context. William Labov pioneered variationist sociolinguistics and real-time language change studies. Linguistics encompasses historical and diachronic study. Language variation is the synchronic diversity underlying language change. Dialects are regional systems that evolve differently over time. Structural linguistics provides the descriptive framework used to analyze language systems as they change. Linguistic relativity relates to how language structures reflect and influence thought. Historical linguistics is the branch studying language change over centuries and millennia. The comparative method is the toolkit for reconstructing unattested ancestral languages from change patterns.
